prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated free of Doppler, recoil and light-shift errors, bringing atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks (B041) for Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye as my final position, and the exchange has made the case firmer rather than merely more popular. Nothing in round 1 disputes the physics. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice is a single identifiable idea that removes the old trade-off between tight confinement and light shifts, and it is what allowed many atoms to be interrogated at once without Doppler or recoil broadening. Ye's group then took stability and accuracy to the 10^-18 regime, used the many-atom and spin-polarised Fermi-gas clocks to expose and control systematics, and showed what the clocks are for: gravitational redshift resolved across millimetres, limits on varying constants and ultralight dark-matter couplings. Independent laboratories in several countries now agree below 10^-18, so maturity is not in doubt. The attribution is the cleanest on the list, as six members name the same pair and none proposes another. On the chair's boundary question, my answer is yes: the citation should be written on the lattice concept and its realisation, and the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems should enter only as enabling background. The citation I propose says so explicitly. I also keep my earlier view that IceCube is a deep discovery in nature, but it fails the test the other members applied and I apply too, namely a defensible cut among hundreds of collaborators and source associations that still await corroboration.
statement.case_against: The serious reservation is the one raised by Lindroth, Mehlig and Johansson and which I raised myself: this is a measurement invention, and a third prize in precision spectroscopy after 2005 and 2012 may look like a lineage already honoured. I think the lattice clock is a distinct step, because it is a different physical regime (many neutral atoms, magic-wavelength trapping) and not a refinement of the comb or of ion control, but a reasonable colleague can weigh it differently, and the committee should state openly that it is rewarding an invention. Second, two names leave out real contributions from Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley and the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups, who were decisive for particular accuracy milestones. Third, part of Ye's record rests on the comb and broader clock programme, so the citation must keep his credit tied to the lattice clock. Fourth, the SI second has not been redefined; I have decided that this is a reason for care in wording, not a reason to wait.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice concept, not combs or ion traps, is the citable discovery, that maturity is not in doubt, and that the redefinition of the second should not govern timing.
responses.response: I agree and I now hold the same view on timing. In round 1 I asked whether the missing redefinition was a reason to wait. On reflection a prize for the lattice clock rests on independently confirmed 10^-18 agreement and on the physics it has already delivered, so it does not depend on a metrological decision taken by another body that could slip for years. I accept your Boulder disclosure as noted and see no need for recusal, since you report no collaboration with Katori or Ye and your judgement of the physics matches that of members with no such tie. On the question of Ye I would answer the chair's question this way: his credit is sufficient and independent of the comb, because the many-body lattice-clock work and the record uncertainties are lattice-clock results, and the proposed citation says so.

responses.point: Lindroth finds the physics of B041 soundly understood but worries that it is a technique with a modest conceptual reorganisation of physics, that it follows the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and that the redefinition of the second is not completed.
responses.response: Your point that the blackbody and level-shift control is understood, not merely demonstrated, is what persuades me on maturity, and as the member least close to atomic structure I rely on it. I disagree somewhat with the conceptual-modesty point: the magic-wavelength condition is a clear conceptual step that changed what a trapped-atom clock could be, and the many-body clock work shows physics, not only engineering. I do take your warning about the earlier prizes seriously, and it is why I have put the lattice and the many-atom regime into the citation. I would be glad to hear whether you think the Paris and NIST contributions you mention are strong enough that two names cannot cover them, because that is the one attribution point that could change my view.

responses.point: Olsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first for field-creating novelty and a clean theory-plus-experiment split, while conceding that she cannot claim B017 is a safer prize than B041.
responses.response: Your candour on safety is helpful, and I think the disagreement really is about weighting. I accept that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the Jarillo-Herrero experiments is a better attribution story than IceCube's. But eight years of reproduction does not settle what the superconductivity is, and the 2018 experiments were carried out by Cao, Fatemi and others who are outside the credited three, so a B017 citation would invite the same questions you accept. I would support it more readily in a few years, and I am willing to be persuaded sooner if a pairing mechanism emerges. For now I keep it as my first alternative and ask whether, given this, you would accept B041 if it prevails.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from altermagnetism to twisted bilayer graphene, regards the theory-plus-experiment attribution as unusually clean, and says he would accept B041 if maturity is judged decisive.
responses.response: I accept that B017 has held up under examination from several sides and that it is a better candidate than B019, which only you have ranked. I still weigh the unresolved pairing mechanism and sample-to-sample variability as a reason for patience, and I note that you share that reservation. On your question of what citation would work, I would anchor it on the flat-band prediction and the observed correlated insulating and superconducting states and say nothing on mechanism; that wording is safe for the physics, though it does not resolve the omission of Cao and Fatemi. Thank you for stating that you would accept B041; I would accept B017 in a later year on the same terms.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from IceCube to B041 but sees IceCube as the discovery in nature and the first alternative to revisit once KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD corroborate source associations.
responses.response: We agree about the science of IceCube and I still regard it as the strongest discovery in nature on this list. Your own point about the drilling, optical-module and calibration teams is the reason I do not put it first now: a two- or three-name credit within a collaboration of hundreds is contestable, and the diffuse flux is established while the source identifications (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) are at modest significance. I have changed my second alternative accordingly. I place B017 before B029 on the current maturity of the evidence, and I would expect IceCube to move up once the Galactic and source results are corroborated by independent detectors.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from fluctuation theorems to B041 and asks the committee to say plainly that it is rewarding a metrology invention and to draw the citation tightly around the lattice concept.
responses.response: I agree with both requests, and I have written the citation on the lattice concept and its realisation, naming the removal of Doppler, recoil and light-shift errors, so it cannot read as a second comb prize. I also agree that the committee should say openly that it rewards an invention, as earlier prizes in this area did. The invention-versus-discovery distinction should not be an exclusion criterion, but a prize for a measurement invention is justified when it changes what can be measured and has delivered new physics, which the lattice clock has. I would not apply the distinction asymmetrically against B041 and in favour of B017.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the boundary against the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems, or prefers a wider clock citation that would require dropping a laureate because of the three-person limit.

Whether Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley or the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups have a claim that two names cannot cover; I rely on the supplied credit and on colleagues' accounts of priority, not an independent check.
How much of Ye's credit rests on the lattice clock rather than the comb and wider clock programme; I judge that it suffices, but this is a judgement about attribution.
Whether the committee still wants to wait for the redefinition of the second, and whether the invention-versus-discovery distinction will be applied evenly.
Whether corroboration of IceCube source associations by KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD, or a pairing mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene, will change the order of the alternatives in coming years.
statement.conflict_note: I have no documented personal or institutional tie to Katori, Ye or any group named for B041, and my preferred configuration lies outside my field of astroparticle and instrument physics. I disclose that IceCube (B029) is in my own field and that I worked with the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and PoGO collaborations, with no documented tie to IceCube or its named individuals, and B029 is only my second alternative. I have noted Kroll's disclosure of his stay in the Hall laboratory at JILA and, with his statement that he has no collaboration with Katori or Ye, I do not consider recusal necessary for him or for any other member on B041 or B017.
